name: Bed rotting

lead: Bed rotting is the practice of voluntarily spending many hours of the day in bed while awake, often with a phone, laptop, TV or a book. Supporters describe it as self-care and recovery from burnout. For appearance, the rest-day chain is more sleep and recovery, which people link to fresher skin, less puffiness and better training results.

In looksmaxxing forums the term more often appears as a habit people want to break, with users describing hours lost to scrolling in bed and low activity. A 2024 survey reported by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found that nearly a quarter of Gen Z respondents had spent a day or more in bed to relax or use devices.

paras: In practice it means staying in bed for a day or a long stretch, often with snacks and a device. Some people schedule it as a recovery day after a hard week; others describe it as a drift they find hard to stop.

Commentators in media coverage say that occasional rest can be fine, while longer stretches that replace outdoor activity, social contact or responsibilities have been linked to poor hygiene, low mood and anxiety. Persistent withdrawal is something clinicians suggest raising with a doctor or therapist.

angle.text: A deliberate rest day can give extra sleep and recovery, which people connect to skin and physique. When it becomes a long, unplanned habit, forum users describe it as taking time from training, going outside and grooming.

lead: Bed rotting is a term, popularised among Gen Z users on TikTok in 2023, for voluntarily spending many hours a day in bed while awake, using a phone, laptop, TV or console, or reading [1]. Dictionary.com defines it as a voluntary withdrawal from activity or stress and added the term in 2024 [1].

People who practise it describe it as rest and a response to burnout and mental fatigue, and Lifehacker connected it to JOMO, the joy of missing out [1]. In looksmaxxing terms the case for it runs through recovery: a rest day leaves room for sleep, which supports skin, and for muscle recovery between training days. The same communities more often discuss the opposite angle, users on looksmax.org asking how to stop it because lost activity and time indoors feel to them like a drag on self-improvement [2].

paras: The term spread on TikTok and was covered in mid-2023 by outlets including Lifehacker, CNN and Forbes [1]. A 2024 survey cited by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine reported that nearly a quarter of Gen Z respondents had stayed in bed for a day or more to relax or use devices [1].
Supporters present bed rotting as short-term rest and self-care, a way to step back from stress and obligations [1]. Lifehacker described it as an aspect of JOMO [1].

No studies found on bed rotting itself. Coverage describes it as a response to stress or anxiety, and Ohio State University's Nicole Hollingshead asked in 2024 whether it is a self-care strategy or a mental health warning sign [1]. Health magazine reported in 2026 that short-term rest may be fine but becomes concerning if it lasts more than a day or two [1].

On looksmax.org a user asked how to stop bed rotting, writing that they spent hours watching videos and scrolling in bed after giving up skating, and that they wanted to change their life but found it hard [2]. Replies in the thread were brief and joking [2].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the habit is mentioned as something to stop rather than a tactic, with jokes about collagen and doctors in replies [2].

claims.claim: Staying in bed all day derails self-improvement.
